item.title: How a small-town P.E.I. trailer maker is fighting back against U.S. tariffs
item.description: An Island trailer manufacturer is shifting its focus to Canadian customers as U.S. tariffs have disrupted its plans for growth.
item.dc:creator: Maria Sarrouh
item.content:encoded: COLEMAN, P.E.I. – An Island trailer manufacturer is shifting its focus to Canadian customers as U.S. tariffs have disrupted its plans for growth. Trout River Industries has struggled since the trade war began, says president Stephen Kennaugh. It has absorbed nearly $1 million in tariff costs, while sales have fallen on both sides of the border. “We’re survivors. So, we’re going to survive anyway,” Kennaugh said. “We have 106 people here and they all have paycheques, they all have mortgages and they all have groceries. We’re responsible for that.” The U.S. once accounted for 40 per cent of Trout River’s sales, with the company pushing for more. Now, every trailer it sells south of the border faces a 25 per cent tariff. The company bears half that cost, while American dealerships and customers cover the rest. Uncertainty is also making it difficult to plan with partners. The manufacturer builds large commercial trailers that use a conveyor belt to unload cargo, rather than tipping up like a dump trailer. They’re particularly popular in the paving industry, though the trailers are also used in agriculture. Trout River is one of 17 Island businesses and organizations awarded non-repayable funding from Ottawa this month through the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. They’re sharing more than $6.9 million to help them respond to U.S. tariffs. A grant of nearly $988,000 will help Trout River pay for a newly completed inventory building, which will allow workers to prepare kits containing all the parts needed for each trailer, so everything arrives together when production begins. Better inventory control will also allow the company to keep less stock on hand. “The efficiency and the cost saving is going to help us to compete,” Kennaugh said. Across the industry, the trade war has taught manufacturers some hard lessons, says Ron Marcolin, the divisional vice-president for New Brunswick and P.E.I. with Canadian Manufacturers and Exporters. “We can’t count on the United States going forward, exclusively. And some companies did that for a number of years,” he said. “Diversification is key.” That rings true on Trout River’s factory floor. Kennaugh still wants to sell as many trailers as possible in the U.S., but hopes growth at home will make those exports a smaller share of the business. In Western Canada, the company is targeting the woodchip and fuel industries with a new trailer design. It’s also exploring tougher models for mines in northern Ontario. But businesses in the region are also looking across the Atlantic Ocean for opportunity. Marcolin says manufacturers are “jumping at the chance” to export to Europe. “We do have a strategic advantage on this coast,” he said. Citing relatively few language barriers, straightforward currency exchanges and Canada’s reputation for quality and timely delivery, Marcolin is optimistic those efforts will be successful.

item.title: Employee arrested after listening device found in OpenAI conference room, FBI and the company say
item.description: An OpenAI engineer has been charged with installing a recording device inside a conference room in what officials said was a bid to capture conversations about the firm’s technology.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: WASHINGTON — An engineer at OpenAI has been charged with secretly installing a recording device inside a conference room in what officials said Tuesday was an effort to capture sensitive conversations about the company’s technology. The employee, identified as a 35-year-old Saudi national named Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested Friday, a week after the ChatGPT maker discovered an audio recording device hidden in the conference room, according to a criminal complaint filed in federal court in San Francisco. The complaint did not identify the company, but the company confirmed in a separate statement that it had discovered a “sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices,” reported the finding to the FBI and fired the employee. “We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work,” an OpenAI spokesperson said. “At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated,” the statement said. The complaint does not detail what Alfozan might have wanted to do with any captured communications. Alfozan made his first court appearance Tuesday on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. It was not immediately clear if he had a lawyer who could speak on his behalf. The recording device was found September 30 concealed in toilet paper and inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in the conference room, according to the complaint. Though the conference room where the recording device was found did not have a camera at the time it was installed, closed-circuit television footage inside the company’s offices revealed that Alfozan was near the conference room on a half-dozen occasions last month despite not having any authority to access the space, the complaint says. The company subsequently added a camera to the room that last week captured Alfozan entering and checking behind the television where the recording device was installed, according to the FBI. The complaint also he also used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about the company’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars. Before his arrest last week, the complaint says, Alfozan left an unattended bag in a different room in the building that included his wallet, identification and another recording device. Eric Tucker, The Associated Press

item.title: Lightspeed cuts 250 roles by laying off staff, not filling vacancies
item.description: Lightspeed Commerce Inc. says 250 roles will be impacted as the company lays off staff and opts to not fill some vacancies.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: Lightspeed Commerce Inc. says 250 roles will be impacted as the company lays off staff and opts to not fill some vacancies. The Montreal-based software business says the cuts are meant to simplify its operations and create room to reinvest in customer growth and product innovations. Spokesperson Stéphanie Princivil did not answer questions about what areas of the company the layoffs and removal of vacancies targeted but said in an email that Lightspeed will provide more information when it reports quarterly earnings next month. Lightspeed has made several staffing cuts over the last few years as Dax Dasilva, Lightspeed’s founder and chief executive, returned to the top job. In hopes of creating more shareholder value, the company also conducted a strategic review, but it concluded last year with no go-private transaction. Instead, the company opted to double down on its North American retail and European hospitality divisions and sell Upserve, a business it owned which offered restaurant management tools. --- Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

item.title: Stelco president responds to demands from Minister Joly
item.description: Stelco Inc. says Canadian exports of cold-rolled and coated steel to the United States have plunged 58 per cent compared with pre-trade-war levels, while continued foreign imports put pressure on ...
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA — Canadian exports of cold-rolled and coated steel to the United States have plunged 58 per cent from pre-trade-war levels as foreign imports continue to undercut Canadian-made steel, Stelco Inc.’s president said in defending plans to lay off up to 500 workers across two Ontario plants. In a seven-page letter to Canada’s industry minister obtained by The Canadian Press, Paul Simon described an industry upended by U.S. tariffs, weakening demand and continued foreign steel imports. “Stelco cannot continue to produce cold-rolled and coated steel products without incurring significant losses that are not sustainable,” Simon said in the letter. “As such, we will continue with the idling of Hamilton Works.” The Oct. 9 letter provides new figures illustrating what Stelco says is a contracting market for its products. Canadian exports of cold-rolled and coated steel to the United States fell by 226,000 tonnes in the second quarter of 2026 compared with the 2024 quarterly average before the trade war began, Simon said. Meanwhile, imports accounted for 45 per cent of market share for those products, despite Ottawa’s efforts to protect domestic producers by restricting steel imports, he said. Simon argued that existing Canadian trade protections are “woefully inadequate” to create a sustainable market that can support two domestic producers of those products. Meanwhile, disruptions to Canadian industries that rely on cold-rolled and coated steel have led to a 10 per cent decline in domestic demand for those products, he said. The letter came in response to Industry Minister Mélanie Joly’s demand that Stelco explain how it will honour employment commitments made by its U.S.-based owner, Cleveland-Cliffs, when it acquired the company in 2024.  Ottawa’s approval of the takeover was contingent on Cleveland-Cliffs maintaining at least the same number of unionized workers and the vast majority of non-unionized employees for five years. Simon, who is also Stelco’s general counsel, said the company is proceeding with plans to idle its Hamilton finishing operations despite Joly’s warning of possible legal action. He argued that the layoffs, which are expected to impact both the Hamilton Works and Lake Erie Works plants, do not violate the company’s binding employment commitments, which he argued do not prohibit layoffs or require employment levels to remain above a specified number every day of the five-year period. Simon said Ottawa was warned as early as July that Stelco might indefinitely idle its Hamilton finishing operations, and that federal officials subsequently suggested discussions about revising the company’s employment commitments to reflect the planned shutdown and layoffs. In a statement posted to X on Oct. 10, Joly said Stelco’s employment commitments remain in force despite changing business strategies or market conditions, adding that all options remain on the table as government lawyers review the company’s response.  Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves has publicly supported U.S. steel tariffs while advocating for a “Fortress North America” approach that would see Canada and the United States impose stronger restrictions on steel imports from outside the continent. Joly had previously said Stelco has “explicitly chosen not to seek support” from government programs designed to preserve jobs and maintain operations. Simon said Ottawa’s offer of financial help did not address the underlying reasons for Stelco’s decision to idle some operations. He said the government offered funding to offset maintenance and capital expenses in exchange for retaining workers, but argued that the assistance would not solve the company’s lack of orders for cold-rolled and coated steel. He characterized the proposal as “a last-ditch effort to cover for an inadequate Canadian trade regime.” Stelco said it is taking steps to ensure its Hamilton finishing operations can restart with “minimal additional costs and time,” but provided no timetable for doing so. --- Brett Bundale, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.
